articles.summary: Middle East News: Iran is tightening its grip on citizens as internal tensions mount, introducing tougher restrictions on communication with foreign media and instituti.
articles.body: Iran is tightening its grip on citizens as internal tensions mount, introducing tougher restrictions on communication with foreign media and institutions amid growing fears of dissent. The latest measures come as the country faces mounting economic pressure, with US sanctions threatening further disruption while the Iranian rial has fallen to a record low, worsening pressure on ordinary Iranians.According to Newsnationâs report, citing NewsNation and regime-monitored Iranian media, Tehran has introduced new regulations criminalising contact with what it describes as âhostileâ media outlets. A bill titled âCountering the Infiltration of Intelligence Services and Foreign Governments or Institutions in the Countryâ reportedly makes interviews with foreign media an offence, specifically naming US and Israeli outlets. Those found sharing information could face up to two years in prison.The measures extend beyond media interactions, with academic cooperation and communication with foreign institutions also potentially coming under scrutiny. An Iranian refugee who spoke to NewsNation anonymously for safety said the rules were designed to prevent Iranians from informing the outside world about abuses and organising future protests.âThese new rules are another attempt by the regime to tighten its control over people and prevent any form of independent connection or cooperation with the outside world,â the refugee said.âThis goes far beyond ordinary regulation or censorship. It is about controlling who people are allowed to communicate and cooperate with, particularly when those connections could expose them to ideas, opportunities, information, or networks outside the regimeâs control,â they added.US sanctions deepen economic pressureThe crackdown comes as Iran faces intensified economic pressure from Washington. The US has announced expanded sanctions targeting Tehran and warned that countries continuing to trade with Iran could also face secondary sanctions. Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei warned that Tehran would respond to any escalation, saying, âOur hands are not tied.âThe pressure is being felt inside Iran, where the currency has hit a record low. While the Iranian economy has adapted to years of sanctions by developing domestic industries and finding alternative trading partners, further restrictions risk pushing up the cost of basic goods and deepening public frustration.Iranian refugee Rayan Amiri, founding leader of the Conservative Party of Iran, said the latest measures reflected a broader strategy of ruling through fear. âThe Islamist regime is afraid that these voices may receive international attention and inform the international community about the dreadful and Orwellian situation in Iran,â Amiri said.He alleged that the regime labels activists and commentators as CIA or Mossad agents and seeks to imprison or assassinate critics abroad. He cited the killings of Iranian exiles Masoud Molavi and Saeed Karimian in Turkey as examples.The crackdown has also extended to people sharing information about unrest. Earlier this month, the Islamic Republicâs judiciary warned that anyone sharing footage or information with âhostile states against national security and interestsâ that causes âpublic panicâ could face the capital charge of âCorruption on Earthâ.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: 'Myanmar's human rights crisis has hit new low': UN flags atrocities against Rohingya
articles.summary: South Asia News: The human rights situation in Myanmar has reached a new low, with widespread atrocities against the Rohingya minority and a rapidly expanding illicit .
articles.body: The human rights situation in Myanmar has reached a new low, with widespread atrocities against the Rohingya minority and a rapidly expanding illicit economy further deepening the suffering of civilians, the United Nations said on Tuesday.According to a report by the UN human rights office covering the period from June 2025 to May 2026, unrelenting conflict, military violence and a growing âconflict economyâ have exposed millions of civilians to severe hardship.Both the Myanmar military and the Arakan Army, which controls large parts of Rakhine State, have been accused of systemic abuses against Rohingya communities. These include killings, torture, forced labour, forced recruitment, arbitrary detention, sexual violence and forced displacement.Nearly nine years after the military crackdown that triggered the mass exodus of Rohingya in 2017, the community continues to face persecution and displacement. The situation has deteriorated further since the military coup in February 2021 that ousted Aung San Suu Kyi and plunged the country into a prolonged civil war.The military-backed electoral process held earlier this year paved the way for junta leader Min Aung Hlaing to become president, while the military continued to consolidate its grip over the country.The UN said the military had continued to use airstrikes, arson and restrictions on humanitarian assistance to terrorise civilians and maintain control. At least 8,075 civilians, including 1,774 women and 1,074 children, have been killed since the 2021 coup, according to UN figures. The actual toll is believed to be significantly higher.Myanmarâs military has denied deliberately targeting civilians, saying its airstrikes were limited to military targets and were carried out in response to armed groups seizing towns and villages. It has also described several of the groups fighting it as terrorist organisations.The conflict has also triggered a massive humanitarian crisis. The number of internally displaced people has risen to about 3.6 million, while an estimated 12.4 million people are facing acute food insecurity. Among those affected are hundreds of thousands of women and children suffering from acute malnutrition.Rohingya caught between two armed forcesThe UN has accused the Arakan Army of carrying out serious abuses against Rohingya communities in northern Rakhine, including arbitrary arrests, torture, sexual abuse and forced labour.The group has also been accused of seizing Rohingya land and preventing displaced people from returning to their homes, while allowing non-Rohingya communities to settle on some confiscated properties.Satellite imagery reviewed by the UN indicates that around 2,000 acres of land have been seized. Witness accounts also describe children as young as six being subjected to forced labour.Former detainees have reported torture in custody, with some inmates allegedly dying as a result of their treatment.The abuses have left the Rohingya trapped between competing armed forces, with neither the military nor the Arakan Army providing meaningful protection from persecution and violence.Myanmarâs hidden mining economyThe conflict has also created a parallel economy that is helping finance armed groups while devastating local communities and the environment.The UN report highlights the rapid expansion of illegal rare-earth mining in Kachin and Shan states, where the collapse of the rule of law has allowed illicit industries to flourish.In Kachin, at least 302 new mining sites have emerged since the 2021 coup. In Shan State, the number of sites has increased from just 12 before the coup to 85.The rare-earth trade reached an estimated peak value of $1.4 billion in 2023, with much of the output flowing into Chinaâs market, according to the UN.But the economic gains have come at a devastating environmental and human cost.Toxic chemicals released during mining have contaminated waterways and farmland, contributing to chronic illnesses and reported miscarriages among communities living near mining areas.The pollution is also crossing national borders. Contaminated water has reached rivers flowing into Thailand, where testing has detected elevated levels of arsenic, lead, mercury and manganese.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Trump eyes changing Lake Ontario name amid trade war with Canada
articles.summary: President Trump said Tuesday his administration is considering changing the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America, amid the trade war between the U.S. and Canada. “The United States is giving serious consideration to changing the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America in that we don’t expect to doing much business with Ontario any…
articles.body:
President Trump said Tuesday his administration is considering changing the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America, amid the trade war between the U.S. and Canada.

“The United States is giving serious consideration to changing the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America in that we don’t expect to doing much business with Ontario any longer,” Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social .

It would not be the first time the president has sought to rename a body of water bordering the U.S. and another country. Last year, Trump signed an executive ordering renaming the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America .

Trade tensions between Washington and Ottawa devolved into an all-out trade war over the weekend after Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney removed negotiators from trade talks with the U.S.

Carney’s move came before a new set of tariffs from the Trump administration on Canada were set to go into effect.

The prime minister then announced that Ottawa would enact retaliatory tariffs in response to the U.S.’s new 50 percent tariffs starting Sept. 8. The Canadian leader said during a press conference that his nation would “match Washington’s new tariffs dollar for dollar in order to protect Canadian workers, farmers, families and businesses.”

Ontario Premier Doug Ford also lashed out at Trump over the levies, threatening on Monday to cut the province’s power exports to the U.S.

“We power 1.5 million homes and businesses,” Ford told reporters Monday. “Everything’s on the table. I’ll do whatever it takes.”

“You won’t get a grain of sand out of Ontario,” he added.

articles.title: A Kansas cowboy put 50 wind turbines on his 7,000-acre ranch and turned the wind into his most reliable cash crop, selling electricity to thousands of homes
articles.summary: US News: A 7,000-acre cattle ranch in Kansas has found an unusual way to generate a steady income alongside traditional ranching. Pete Ferrell, a fourth-genera.
articles.body: A 7,000-acre cattle ranch in Kansas has found an unusual way to generate a steady income alongside traditional ranching. Pete Ferrell, a fourth-generation rancher, hosts 50 industrial wind turbines on his property as part of the 100-turbine Elk River Wind Project, a 150-megawatt facility that began operating in 2005. The turbines do not replace the cattle or transform the entire ranch into an energy facility. Instead, cattle continue to graze across much of the tallgrass prairie while the wind project provides Ferrell with lease income. The facility also generates enough electricity to serve tens of thousands of homes based on its original production estimates. What began as a source of concern for Ferrell eventually became an important financial cushion, particularly during droughts when traditional ranching income can become unpredictable.A Kansas cowboy turns 50 wind turbines into a new cash cropThe Ferrell family's connection to wind power began long before today's giant turbines appeared across Kansas. In 1923, Ferrell's great-grandfather installed a Jacobs Windjammer wind turbine paired with a Delco glass battery at the ranch, providing electricity before the electrical grid reached the property. Nearly a century later, Pete Ferrell faced a very different proposal when developers approached him about installing commercial wind turbines. He initially rejected the idea because he feared the machines would damage the prairie and interfere with the ranching operation. A visit to California's Altamont Pass changed his perspective after he saw ranchers continuing to care for their land while turbines operated around them. The experience helped convince Ferrell that wind energy could coexist with cattle ranching, eventually leading him to lease part of his property for the Elk River Wind Project.Fifty turbines are part of a 100-turbine wind farmThe 50 turbines on Ferrell's property represent only half of the Elk River Wind Project. Kansas state records describe the facility as a 150-megawatt wind farm containing 100 GE 1.5-megawatt turbines in Butler County near Beaumont. The remaining turbines are located on neighbouring properties. The project began commercial operation in December 2005 and was originally expected to generate about 550,000 megawatt-hours of electricity each year. At the time, developers estimated that output would be equivalent to the electricity consumption of roughly 42,000 homes annually. The actual amount of electricity produced varies depending on wind conditions, so the figure should be understood as an annual estimate rather than a fixed number of homes receiving power directly from Ferrell's turbines. The electricity enters the regional power system, while Ferrell receives income from leasing his land to the project.Wind became a reliable source of ranch incomeThe biggest attraction for Ferrell was not simply the electricity produced by the turbines but the additional income generated by leasing his land. Wind royalties have become an important part of the ranch's finances, providing a source of revenue that does not depend directly on cattle prices, grass production or rainfall. Ferrell has described wind as his "best insurance policy" because the payments continue even during difficult agricultural years. Drought can reduce forage across the Flint Hills and force ranchers to reduce livestock numbers or spend more money on feed, while the turbines can continue producing electricity as long as suitable winds are available. The arrangement effectively allows the same land to generate two forms of economic value. Cattle continue to provide the traditional agricultural income, while the wind project provides lease payments. The Environmental Defense Fund has highlighted Ferrell's experience as an example of how renewable-energy development can provide financial stability for rural landowners.Cattle still graze around the turbinesThe presence of 50 industrial turbines has not ended the ranch's traditional agricultural operation. Cattle continue to graze across much of the property, including areas surrounding the turbine infrastructure. Ferrell has said that roughly 50 acres of the ranch became unavailable for grazing because of turbine foundations, roads and related infrastructure. That represents only a small portion of a property covering about 7,000 acres. The arrangement allows Ferrell to maintain cattle production while earning additional revenue from the wind project. This is particularly significant in the Flint Hills, where ranching depends heavily on the health of native tallgrass prairie and seasonal weather conditions. Wind development therefore became an additional layer of income rather than a replacement for agriculture. Ferrell's experience shows why some rural landowners view turbines differently from people who see them only as large industrial structures. On a working ranch, the infrastructure can occupy a relatively small part of the property while providing payments over many years.The project brought wider economic benefits to the regionElk River is part of Kansas's much larger wind-energy industry, which has brought significant investment and lease payments to rural communities. Wind projects can generate revenue for landowners while also contributing to local tax bases, construction activity and employment. Kansas has become one of the leading wind-energy states in the US because of its strong wind resources and large areas of relatively open land. The economic benefits, however, come alongside genuine debates about where turbines should be built. Residents and landowners can raise concerns about views, wildlife, noise, roads, transmission infrastructure and changes to rural landscapes. Those issues are particularly important in the Flint Hills because the region contains some of the largest remaining areas of tallgrass prairie in North America. Ferrell's experience should therefore not be treated as evidence that every ranch is suitable for wind development. Instead, it shows how carefully planned projects can coexist with agricultural operations and give landowners another source of income.The wind became another cash crop without replacing the cattleNearly two decades after the Elk River Wind Project began operating, Ferrell's ranch remains a working cattle operation with 50 turbines standing across its prairie. The electricity generated by those turbines is sold into the regional power system, rather than directly by Ferrell to individual households, while his income comes from leasing his land to the wind project. That distinction does not make the financial transformation any less remarkable. The ranch has effectively found a way to make the same landscape produce two different sources of economic value. Cattle still depend on grass, rainfall and market conditions, while the wind turbines provide a separate stream of lease revenue. The arrangement also reflects a much longer family relationship with wind power that began with a small turbine and battery in 1923. Almost a century later, the Ferrell family is still drawing value from the Kansas wind, only now on a vastly larger scale.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Andrew Tate exaggerates and does not own supercars in photos, lawyers claim
articles.summary: Prosecutors argue Tate and his brother Tristan are a flight risk and should not be released on bail.
articles.body:
Controversial influencer Andrew Tate portrays himself as "uberwealthy" but did not own cars and a yacht featured on his social media and exaggerated his lifestyle for online attention, his legal representatives have said.

Tate and his brother Tristan are currently being held in a Florida jail but are seeking release on bail while they await the outcome of extradition proceedings.

They were arrested last month after British prosecutors unveiled new charges including alleged sexual offences against them, which both men deny.

Prosecutors have argued the Tates are a "flight risk", citing the brothers' past statements about their wealth and influence and having multiple identities to evade the law.

In a legal submission to the court, the brothers' legal representatives said the Tates' business model "depends on online attention".

"The outrageousness of the posts by them and about them is the point. The more hyperbolic and outlandish the post, the more likely it will generate views and likes, which in turn generates income. In short, they are playing a role," it says.

At times Andrew Tate has also exaggerated and used hyperbole for "comedic effect" with no intention to be taken seriously, the submission argues.

"The government alleges that the Tates are a risk of flight based on their social media claims that they are 'self-proclaimed billionaires' who own 'high-end vehicles, private jets, and a custom $50-million-dollar superyacht and have unrestricted access to traditional funds, cryptocurrency, and bitcoin,'" it says.

"But the government has not established these grandiose claims are true," it adds.

Prosecutors argued that both brothers "have significant resources available to them, both in terms of money and in social media networks," adding they also have shown a "propensity to intimidate vulnerable complainants".

Prosecutors also cited social media posts made by Andrew Tate, in which he allegedly mocked prosecutors and suggested he could hide his identity to avoid arrest.

The superyacht referenced is not owned by the Tates and they were paid to promote it, the submission says.

Cars, including an Aston Martin and Bugattis which featured in social media content, were rented, it says.

"The Tates are engaged in several businesses 'teaching' men how to earn money. It is in their interest to portray themselves on social media as uberwealthy," it adds.

US Marshals arrested the brothers in Miami last month after the Crown Prosecution Service in the UK brought 38 new charges, including rape and offences related to sex trafficking, against them.

They are now facing a total of 59 charges relating to alleged offences between July 2010 and August 2017.

Andrew, 39, and Tristan, 38, have both previously denied any wrongdoing.

The brothers are dual British-US citizens and spent part of their childhood in Luton.

Self-proclaimed "misogynist" Tate first rose to fame after an appearance on the British version of reality TV show Big Brother in 2016.

A former kickboxer, he has millions of social media followers and has appeared in countless videos flaunting what appears to be an ultra-luxurious lifestyle.

articles.title: Trump hopes sanctions will topple Iran's regime - its leaders are betting otherwise
articles.summary: The US says new sanctions are an "economic D-Day", but Tehran's leaders have survived restrictions before.
articles.body:
The US says it has launched an "economic onslaught against Iran's financial connections around the globe". Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said sanctions included digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping. Any nation financially partnering with Iran would be isolated.

However, Bessent's announcement of what he termed an "economic D-Day" may have sounded more dramatic in Washington than in Tehran.

Shortly after the announcement, Iran's Economy Minister Ali Madanizadeh called it "the same old talk" and said Iran was ready for "every scenario". He said Tehran had expected the measures and had plans to deal with them.

His reaction points to the main question Iranian leaders are likely to be asking: What can the US do now that it has not already tried?

Bessent has threatened wider secondary sanctions against countries, banks and companies that continue doing business with Iran. But the basic policy is not new. Iran has faced US sanctions for years, including penalties against foreign companies trading with it.

What matters to Tehran is whether Washington can enforce sanctions more widely than before.

The US blockade has already made a difference. It has reduced Iran's ability to export as much oil by sea as it did before and made it harder to import goods and equipment. Iran has long land borders with seven countries and years of experience using them to bypass sanctions. But land routes cannot easily replace trade by sea, especially oil exports.

The pressure could therefore become much more serious if Washington manages to close channels that survived previous sanctions, particularly those involving China and Iran's neighbours. That is a big ask. China's foreign ministry said on Tuesday that it firmly opposed the sanctions, calling them illegal.

If the sanctions fail, Bessent's announcement could strengthen those inside Iran who oppose a deal with the US.

They could argue that Washington has returned to economic pressure because its other choices are limited. A new military campaign carries risks, while years of sanctions have failed to force Iran to accept US demands.

Washington has also left little room for diplomacy.

Although Pakistan and other mediators are still trying to revive talks, the US has not ruled out further strikes. The renewed threats could weaken Iranian officials who favour a deal.

It was already in deep trouble before the war, with high inflation and a rapidly weakening currency, and has deteriorated further since the fighting began with US and Israeli air strikes on 28 February.

The weakening of the Iranian currency, the rial, is felt sharply and widely. Imports cost more, businesses struggle to plan, and people's savings lose value. Restrictions on oil exports also reduce the government's access to foreign currency.

Negin - not her real name - is a 34-year-old woman who says her monthly income is now about $100 (£73). She told the BBC: "I don't go to the cinema, theatre, or concerts. I don't buy gifts for anyone. I don't attend birthday parties. I can only buy meat with the government subsidy voucher; otherwise, I wouldn't be able to afford it."

Mona, a housewife with two kids, says her husband has been out of work since the beginning of the war. She adds: "We feel scared, especially after the sanctions that began yesterday. Ever since the war, my spouse has not gone back to work. He used to work on ships."

She adds: "We're trying to manage our expenses as best we can, but we've definitely had to cut back on all of our extra spending and small luxuries."

Iran may believe time is working against US President Donald Trump. Further disruption in the Strait of Hormuz could push oil and petrol prices higher, add to US inflation and become a political problem before the US midterm elections in November.

That gives Tehran an obvious date to watch, but relying on American elections is a gamble.

Iran's economy could be much weaker by then.

And beyond the midterms lies another problem. With Trump not seeking re-election in 2028, his outgoing administration may feel it has more freedom to continue the confrontation with Iran and accept the costs.

Iran is, therefore, watching two clocks.

One is political and runs in Washington. The other is economic and runs inside Iran. Every month of lower oil exports, disrupted trade and pressure on the rial makes waiting for a deal to end the war more expensive.

That leaves Iranian leaders with a difficult choice. Making concessions now could look like surrendering under pressure and strengthen hardliners who say Washington will only demand more.

Waiting could improve Iran's position if Trump's strategy runs into political or economic problems. But Tehran could also find itself negotiating later with a weaker economy.

Much now depends on what happens outside Iran.

If Chinese banks, regional trading partners and companies start pulling back because they believe Washington will punish them, Bessent's campaign may change Tehran's calculation.

If they do not, the opposite could happen. Those Iranians arguing against compromise will say Washington has played another supposedly decisive card without changing the balance and that Iran should continue to wait or resist.

How much could Trump's 'economic D-Day' hurt Iran?

articles.title: Father's house was rammed by car before son died in A66 crash
articles.summary: The house belonging to Cole Worthy's father is significantly damaged and its windows are smashed.
articles.body:
A house rammed by a car before the fatal A66 crash in Middlesbrough belonged to the father of a teenager who died in the incident.

Cole Worthy, 17, was one of five young men who died when a Volkswagen Passat travelling in the wrong direction hit a Cleveland Police armed response vehicle, also killing two police officers.

Before the crash at 03:39 BST on Saturday, police had received multiple reports of two cars driving dangerously around the town and a Volvo XC60 was seen ramming properties.

The BBC understands that, after his father's home was rammed, Worthy and the four others set out in the Passat. Police said they were linking the activities of the Volvo XC60 and the Passat.

There is no suggestion Worthy's father was involved in criminal activity.

PC Tom Clough, 38, and PC Matthew Blades, 37, died in the crash , as did Michael Robert Cahill, 23, Jacob Matusiak, 23, Makai Saddington, 18, Theo Rae, 17, and Worthy.

The Independent Office for Police Conduct said officers had been pursuing the Passat for almost seven minutes after it was connected to earlier alleged criminal activity, but the pursuit was abandoned 10 seconds before the crash when it turned on to the dual carriageway.

Both vehicles were operating with cloned number plates but were picked up by automated number plate recognition technology.

The rammed house is a red bricked semi-detached that sits in a quiet residential street in Acklam.

The downstairs bay window has been smashed, with bricks scattered beneath it, and an upstairs bedroom window has also been broken.

Neighbours, who did not want to be identified, said Worthy sometimes stayed at his father's property.

Locals described hearing loud bangs at around two in the morning on Saturday and said the street had been full of police all weekend.

Meanwhile, nine men and three women, aged between 18 and 61, were arrested across Teesside on Monday as part of the investigation into the lead-up to the crash. They were held on a range of offences, including possession of a firearm and being part of an organised crime group.

Kai Beattie, of Foxrush Court, Redcar, has been charged with possession of a firearm with intent to endanger life.

Cameron George, of Micklow Close, Redcar, has been charged with possession of class A and class B drugs with intent to supply, and possession of criminal property.

Cleveland Police said on Tuesday that five further arrests had been made, including a 16-year-old boy and two men, 18 and 21, who were held on suspicion of participating in an organised crime group.

A 55-year-old man was also arrested on suspicion of assisting an offender and a 23-year-old man on suspicion of making threats to kill.

Those previously arrested as part of the investigation are:

Three men, aged 24, 19 and 35, all held on suspicion of participating in an organised crime group and possession of an offensive weapon. They are in police custody.

A man, 21, held on suspicion of participating in an organised crime group, possession of an offensive weapon and criminal damage. He has been remanded on recall to prison

A 30-year-old woman arrested on suspicion of assisting an offender and who is in police custody

A 20-year-old man arrested on suspicion of threats to cause criminal damage and public order. He remains in custody

A 26-year-old man was charged with possession with intent to supply class A drugs, as well as the possession of criminal property. He was remanded in custody ahead of his next court hearing

Another man, 39, and a 47-year-old woman have been released on conditional bail after both being arrested on suspicion of possessing a firearm without a certificate, possession with intent to supply class A and class B drugs, and possession of class C drugs

An 18-year-old man has been released on unconditional bail after being arrested on suspicion of possessing a firearm without a certificate, possession with intent to supply class A and class B drugs, and possession of class C drugs

A 61-year-old woman has been released on conditional bail after being arrested on suspicion of possessing a firearm without a certificate

A 39-year-old man has been arrested on suspicion of threats to kill and has been released on conditional bail

articles.title: Record heatwaves kill more than 35,000 across Europe, toll expected to rise: Report
articles.summary: Europe News: At least 35,000 excess deaths have happened across Europe during four record-breaking heatwaves this summer, according to a report by the Guardian. Th.
articles.body: At least 35,000 excess deaths have happened across Europe during four record-breaking heatwaves this summer, according to a report by the Guardian. The actual toll is likely to be significantly higher, with August data still unavailable for several countries and heat-related deaths often taking weeks or months to formally identify.Germany, France and Spain alone have recorded more than 25,000 excess deaths. Germany has reported the highest toll, with the Robert Koch Institute estimating around 14,000 heat-related deaths between April 6 and August 9, the country's highest figure since records began.The consecutive heatwaves began in May and pushed temperatures to unprecedented levels across western Europe.France recorded its hottest national average day on record, while more than 500 French weather stations recorded temperatures above 40°C. Germany saw 46 stations cross 40°C in late June, while parts of Spain experienced prolonged temperatures above 42°C.Germany's toll was particularly severe in late June, when the Robert Koch Institute estimated that 9,600 people died during the week of June 22-28. The country's previous annual high for heat-related deaths was 8,900 in 2018, while normal summers typically see fewer than 2,000 such deaths.Spain's mortality monitoring system has attributed 4,947 deaths to heat since May, already surpassing the previous record of 4,520 recorded in 2022. In France, preliminary figures showed 7,300 excess deaths between late May and July 22, although the data covered only about 80% of total mortality and did not include August.Other countries have also reported significant increases. England's health security agency estimated that the May and June heatwaves were linked to 2,877 deaths. Belgium recorded 1,222 excess deaths during an 11-day period in June, while the Netherlands reported at least 900 additional deaths between June 22 and July 5. Modelling estimated another 1,070 excess deaths in Poland during the late-June heatwave.The figures are difficult to establish because heat is rarely recorded as the direct cause of death. Extreme temperatures can worsen existing cardiovascular, respiratory and kidney conditions, with the resulting heart attacks, strokes or organ failures recorded as the immediate causes of death.Experts expect the European death toll to rise as countries consolidate their figures.Italy, for instance, has not yet released a final national estimate, although modelling has suggested that between 5,000 and 8,000 heat-related deaths could eventually be recorded.Scientists have linked the increasingly frequent and intense heatwaves to human-driven global warming. The World Health Organisation said in May that heat-related mortality in its European region had risen by more than 30% over the past two decades and warned that the toll could increase further as the climate crisis intensifies and Europe's population ages.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: IShowSpeedâs $10,000 challenge goes viral after participant lifts 20kg cube in under 5 minutes
articles.summary: US Streamers News: IShowSpeedâs $10,000 challenge quickly turned into a surprise moment after a participant managed to lift a heavy 20kg cube in less than five minutes. .
articles.body: IShowSpeedâs $10,000 challenge quickly turned into a surprise moment after a participant managed to lift a heavy 20kg cube in less than five minutes. The popular streamer had set up a simple public challenge: anyone who could lift the cube could win $10,000. The metal cube weighed about 45 pounds and had no handle, making it much harder to grab than a normal weight. Several people tried and failed, including some strong-looking contestants. However, one young participant stepped up and completed the challenge almost immediately.IShowSpeedâs $10,000 cube challenge ends in just minutesThe challenge looked simple at first. A large metal cube was placed on the ground, and a sign offered $10,000 to anyone who could lift it.The cube weighed around 20 kilograms, or about 45 pounds. But it did not have a handle, bar, or any grooves to hold. Contestants had to use just their hand to grab the smooth cube and lift it from the ground.Several people gave it a try but could not complete the challenge. Some of the contestants were bigger and looked strong enough to lift the weight. Still, the shape of the cube made the task much harder.Then, within the first five minutes, a young participant stepped forward.He grabbed the cube with one hand and pulled it up from the ground. As the cube came higher, he moved his hand underneath it and pulled it closer to his body. He kept control of the weight and did not drop it.The lift was complete, meaning he had earned the $10,000 prize.IShowSpeed stunned by participantâs unusual method to lift 20kg cubeIShowSpeed appeared shocked when the participant completed the challenge so quickly. He even asked people around him if the attempt should count.The short discussion was about how the participant lifted the cube. Some viewers felt that moving his palm underneath the cube made the lift easier than simply pinching the cube with his fingers.However, the challenge only appeared to require contestants to âlift the cube.â There was no clear rule saying that the participant could not move his hand underneath it.Speed and his team eventually accepted the attempt and declared the participant the winner. Speed then ran over to celebrate with him.The challenge also showed why a 20kg cube can feel much harder than a 20kg dumbbell. A dumbbell has a handle that makes it easy to hold. articles.title: Sudan civil war: Trump envoy calls for country-wide arms embargo as drone attacks escalate
articles.summary: A wider arms embargo would require a UN Security Council vote - and Russia and China oppose the move.
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump's senior Africa envoy has asked the UN to extend its arms embargo from Darfur to all of Sudan, warning the war could spread across the wider region.

The UN Security Council "must act to stop external financial and military support to the parties, such as drones and related technologies, from entering Sudan," Massad Boulos said.

Drone attacks are escalating with both the army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) accused of using them. Now in its fourth year, the conflict has killed tens of thousands of people and forced 14 million more to flee their homes.

But a wider arms embargo would require a Security Council vote, with Russia and China opposing the move.

They said it would affect Sudan's army's effectiveness. Sudan's UN envoy agreed, adding it would weaken protection for civilians.

The army controls much of Sudan's central and eastern regions, while the RSF is headquartered in the western region of Darfur and also controls areas in the south.

As the UN Security Council heard appeals about the arms embargo, the army was reported to have carried out drone strikes on RSF positions in Nyala in Darfur.

Nyala airport has become one of the paramilitary group's chief logistics hubs - and the attack came hours after a large cargo flight landed in the city.

The devastating conflict where both sides have reasons to keep fighting

Sudan's invisible children - born in war with no legal identity

An arms embargo covering the Darfur region has been in place for more than two decades - and will expire next month if not amended or renewed.

Observers say it seems to have done little to stop the flow of weapons into Darfur, which has witnessed some of the worst fighting since the conflict erupted in April 2023.

Ethnic violence witnessed 20 years ago has reignited in Darfur, with UN experts saying atrocities allegedly committed by RSF fighters as they took over the city of el-Fasher last October showed the "hallmarks" of genocide.

At the council meeting, UN's humanitarian chief, Tom Fletcher, warned that fighting had in recent weeks been "characterised by the heavy use of drones".

Rosemary DiCarlo, the UN's under secretary-general for political and peacebuilding affairs, told the council that civilians were facing "the unrelenting consequences of one of the worst humanitarian crises of our time".

"Drones launched by both sides have repeatedly struck markets, schools, fuel stations and water infrastructure," she said, adding that the UN had documented that 1,100 civilians had died in drone strikes between January and June this year.

DiCarlo noted that the true death toll since the war began was uncertain but was "likely to be in the hundreds of thousands".

The continued use of "sophisticated weaponry" pointed to ongoing external support to both sides, she added.

Boulos said the US plan included a proposal to increase the number of experts monitoring the embargo.

He asked the council to take steps to curtail "external actors" fuelling the conflict, adding that this "risks drawing more regional actors and neighbours deeper into Sudan's conflict".

Sudan's military chief seemed unfazed by the proposals under discussion by the UN.

"The continuing talk about the possibility of imposing sanctions on the country will neither affect us nor weaken our resolve," Gen Abdel Fattah al-Burhan told a police graduation event in the capital, Khartoum, on Monday.

The flow of weapons into Sudan has been analysed by various experts.

Amnesty International has in the past said it found evidence of weapons manufactured in Serbia, Russia, China, Turkey, Yemen and United Arab Emirates (UAE) being used in Sudan.

The UAE in particular is accused of being the main provider of arms and support to the RSF, who in turn is accused of using the UAE as a marketplace for illicit gold sales. Both parties have repeatedly denied these allegations.

Sudan's military has used Turkish and Iranian drones, and it receives political and other backing from Egypt, Qatar and Saudi Arabia.

The two warring rivals had been allies - coming to power together in a coup in 2021 - but fell out over an internationally backed plan to move towards civilian rule.

articles.title: In 2014, a Texas coalition bought a 17,351-acre coastal ranch for $37.7 million, much of it using Deepwater Horizon restoration money; 15,000 acres later became a wildlife area protecting wetlands, prairie and endangered whooping crane habitat
articles.summary: US News: In 2014, a coalition of conservation groups in Texas completed the purchase of 17,351 acres of coastal land in Calhoun County. Known as Powderhorn Ran.
articles.body: In 2014, a coalition of conservation groups in Texas completed the purchase of 17,351 acres of coastal land in Calhoun County. Known as Powderhorn Ranch, the property was one of the largest remaining areas of unspoiled coastal prairie in the state. The land was bought for $37.7 million, while the wider conservation project was planned at $50 million, including habitat restoration, management and a long-term endowment.According to Texas Tribune, a major part of the money came from funds linked to the Deepwater Horizon oil spill. The National Fish and Wildlife Foundation (NFWF) committed $34.5 million from its Gulf Environmental Benefit Fund. The fund was created using money paid by BP and Transocean after the 2010 oil spill. At the time, the Powderhorn purchase was the largest land acquisition in the US using BP spill restoration money.The purchase was the result of a partnership involving the Texas Parks and Wildlife Foundation, Texas Parks and Wildlife Department, NFWF, The Conservation Fund and The Nature Conservancy of Texas. The organisations had been working towards protecting Powderhorn Ranch for years. The transaction itself had taken more than two years to put together.The land was important also because of the habitats it contained. The ranch included coastal live oak forests, freshwater wetlands, salt marshes and more than 11 miles of tidal bay frontage along Matagorda Bay. The area provided habitat for hundreds of species of birds and animals, including the endangered whooping crane.The long road to protecting PowderhornThe effort to protect Powderhorn Ranch had been considered for more than 30 years by conservation groups and wildlife agencies. Before the purchase, the ranch had passed through several owners and had been reduced to about half of its original size.The owners at the time were Cumberland & Western Resources, LLC. Its main investors were conservation-minded citizens. They agreed to sell the property below its market value to help ensure that it would be protected.âThe acquisition of Powderhorn Ranch will help define the next generation of conservation in Texas,â said TPW Commission Chairman Dan Allen Hughes Jr.Texas had lost more than 200,000 acres of coastal wetlands between the 1950s and early 1990s, according to the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department. The Powderhorn acquisition was presented as one way to counter that loss by keeping a large area of coastal habitat protected.âThe unspoiled and irreplaceable Powderhorn Ranch is now a significant property for all Texans, and a protected national treasure,â said Larry Selzer, CEO of The Conservation Fund.15,000 plus acres become wildlife areaThe conservation project moved into its next stage in October 2018, when more than 15,000 acres of Powderhorn Ranch were transferred to the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department. The land became a state wildlife management area.The transfer marked the completion of a multi-year, $37.7 million land acquisition deal. It also meant that the largest part of the ranch could be managed as protected wildlife habitat.âOur primary management objectives right now focus on the restoration of native grassland and savannah, and for improving existing hydrology to enhance freshwater wetlands habitat for wildlife, particularly whooping cranes that have expanded onto the property,â said Dan Walker, area manager at Powderhorn WMA.The new wildlife management area was also intended to provide public recreation. Hunting, fishing, hiking, paddling and bird watching were among the activities planned for the property.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Trump: French language not a factor in Canada trade talks
articles.summary: President Trump said Tuesday that Canada’s French language requirements are not a factor in the escalating trade tensions between Washington and Ottawa, contradicting Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney. “I would never interfere with Canadians speaking French! In fact, I have never even thought of doing such a stupid thing,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. “This…
articles.body:
President Trump said Tuesday that Canada’s French language requirements are not a factor in the escalating trade tensions between Washington and Ottawa, contradicting Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney.

“I would never interfere with Canadians speaking French! In fact, I have never even thought of doing such a stupid thing,” Trump wrote on Truth Social . “This lie was made up by a weak and ineffective Prime Minister in an attempt to gain political support, which he has totally lost, from the people of Quebec. I love French Canadians!”

His comments echo those from U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, who told CNBC the Canadian claim that French language requirements were a sticking point was a “funny, fake story.”

Carney said Monday that Canada could not accept Washington’s proposed trade deal given its demands to roll back French language requirements.

“We were ready and close to having a comprehensive agreement that would be fair to both countries. But they made changes, including threats on the French language and Quebec culture and Canadian culture,” the prime minister said during a press conference, speaking in French.

“That is not acceptable. That would never be acceptable,” he added.

Canada’s French language requirements have been considered a trade barrier in the U.S. given the added costs and efforts of redesigning packaging to include French labels.

However, the issue is of paramount importance in Canada, particularly in the province of Quebec, where French is the primary language.

articles.title: In 1932, an Ohio foundry worker lost his job and began building a rock garden; he spent 12 years creating hundreds of structures, and his wife preserved it for another 53 years
articles.summary: US News: When Harry George \"Ben\" Hartman lost his job as an iron moulder at the Springfield Machine Tool Company during the Great Depression, he picked up a tr.
articles.body: When Harry George "Ben" Hartman lost his job as an iron moulder at the Springfield Machine Tool Company during the Great Depression, he picked up a trowel and began digging a small concrete fishing pond in his backyard. That simple project soon grew across his entire residential lot. Over 12 years, Hartman built a huge folk art environment using more than 250,000 stones, concrete, metal scraps, wood and recycled glass. After his death in 1944, his wife Mary cared for the entire complex on her own for 53 years, protecting what became one of the leading folk art environments in the United States. According to documentation from the Friends of the Hartman Rock Garden and the Kohler Foundation, the property at 1905 Russell Avenue contains dozens of detailed stone structures, miniature landmarks and hundreds of hand-painted figures representing American history, religion, patriotism and popular culture.From factory job to backyard creationBorn in Edenville, Pennsylvania, in 1882, Hartman moved to Springfield, Ohio, in 1912 to work in the city's heavy machinery foundries. The economic collapse of 1932 ended his industrial career. Suddenly unemployed, Hartman turned his energy towards physical work and began transforming his suburban backyard into a massive construction project. Educational materials prepared for tours of the site say Hartman collected materials from nearby creek beds, rubbish dumps and gravel roads. He often asked his children to collect unusual stones, while friends and local visitors brought discarded glass bottles and pieces of ceramics that he used in the structures. Hartman spent long hours building the garden even after developing severe silicosis, a lung disease caused by years of exposure to dust in foundries. When he died from the illness in 1944 at the age of 61, the garden had spread across the entire residential yard.Architecture, patriotism and personal expressionThe centrepiece of the garden is the Tree of Life, a seven-foot concrete structure covered with river gravel and polished stones. Its branches hold miniature versions of a schoolhouse and church, while two doves of peace sit on either side and a carved American eagle stands at the top. Historical archives maintained by SPACES (Saving and Preserving Arts and Cultural Environments) show that Hartman also built several large architectural replicas directly on the lawn. One of the largest is The Cathedral, a 14-foot-high medieval-style stone building with detailed arches, niches and handmade figures of Jesus, Mary and several saints. The garden also contains scale models of Mount Vernon and the White House, as well as a replica of the Independence Hall clock tower. Hartman created other structures honouring figures including Abraham Lincoln, George Washington and Charles Lindbergh. The garden also includes stone versions of Noah's Ark and covered wagons representing the Oregon Trail. Other parts of the garden show everyday American life, with miniature stone houses, bridges and working water wheels. "This is where it all began, this is the Hobby gone wild," folk art collector Mark Chepp said during a historical tour recorded by public radio station WYSO. "Ben was a pacifist, and as you go through the garden and get involved and start looking at it, you see social commentary that comes through in a number of the objects."53 years of careAfter Hartman's death in 1944, his wife Mary took responsibility for the garden. For the next 53 years, she cut the lawns, cared for the flower beds, repaired damaged concrete and welcomed thousands of visitors who came to see the unusual garden along Russell Avenue. Mary continued giving visitors self-guided tours and showing them around the property until her death in 1997 at the age of 91. In 2008, the Kohler Foundation, a Wisconsin-based non-profit organisation focused on preserving visionary art environments, bought the property from the Hartman family estate. The foundation then began a major restoration project. Workers repaired damaged concrete, strengthened fragile stone structures and catalogued thousands of individual objects. In 2009, ownership was formally transferred to the Friends of the Hartman Rock Garden, a local non-profit organisation created to manage the site, maintain its seasonal flower displays and provide free public tours throughout the year. According to site curator Kevin Rose, writing in an interpretive study for SPACES, the garden remains freely open to visitors every day of the year. Tens of thousands of people from around the world visit the site to see the handmade legacy left behind by an unemployed foundry worker who turned his backyard into a remarkable work of folk art.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Israeli forces raid UNRWA training centre in occupied East Jerusalem
articles.summary: Israeli forces raid and seize the Qalandiya Training Centre, a key UNRWA facility, in the Kafr Aqab neighbourhood.
articles.body:
Israeli forces have raided the Qalandiya Training Centre, a key facility operated by the United Nations agency for Palestinian refugees (UNRWA) in the neighbourhood of Kafr Aqab in occupied East Jerusalem.

Before the raid on Tuesday, which UNRWA condemned, Israeli forces closed the nearby Qalandiya checkpoint, the primary Israeli checkpoint between East Jerusalem and the northern West Bank.

Heavy military deployments spread throughout the surrounding neighbourhoods and the adjacent Qalandiya refugee camp in the occupied West Bank. Soldiers forcibly expelled all UNRWA employees from the site, telling them not to return. Five Palestinians were injured by Israeli gunfire near the training site in Qalandiya, according to the Jerusalem governorate.

Far-right Israeli National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir participated in the raid. Speaking from the site, Ben-Gvir praised the operation, stating that authorities had begun an “operation to evacuate the building” and asserting that “there is no place for the agency in Jerusalem and Israel.” He also posted on X that “UNRWA in our hands.”

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said the incursion was lawful. In a post on X, he said: “In accordance with my directive and following the law we passed, the evacuation of the UNRWA compound in Kafr Aqab, Jerusalem, began today.”

After the raid, the Israeli Ministry of Foreign Affairs announced that the Jerusalem Municipality had already commenced work to transform the property into a new educational and community complex.

The ministry claimed the project would serve thousands of Palestinian residents in Kafr Aqab with facilities including schools, a mosque, sports grounds and health centres.

UNRWA released a statement to “unequivocally condemn” what it described as an “unauthorised and deeply concerning incursion”.

“The entry of armed security forces into a United Nations facility, without the authorisation or consent of the United Nations, is unacceptable,” it said. “The KTC [Qalandiya Training Centre] is a United Nations facility protected by the privileges and immunities afforded to the Organisation under international law. Its inviolability must be fully respected.”

UNRWA also called on the international community to act immediately and condemn the violation.

“The international community must ensure that United Nations premises are protected from unauthorised entry and seizure, and that UNRWA can continue delivering essential services to Palestine Refugee communities without intimidation, obstruction or interference,” UNRWA said.

“The integrity and inviolability of United Nations premises cannot be conditional. They must be respected, upheld and protected.”

Speaking to Al Jazeera, the director of UNRWA affairs in the West Bank, Roland Friedrich, said the break-in was a “very concerning development” and “not just a violation of the privileges and communities of the United Nations” but also a “violation of the right of young Palestinians to quality education”.

Israeli officials alleged that the site had been owned by the Jewish National Fund since 1937 and had been allocated to the Jerusalem Municipality for the educational and community project, arguing that UNRWA had fenced off the land for decades without legal ownership rights. The Foreign Ministry directly cited anti-UNRWA legislation passed by the Israeli Knesset in October 2024, banning the agency’s activities in Israel, to justify the takeover.

UNRWA, however, firmly rejected the claims, maintaining that the Qalandiya Training Centre is a UN facility and is protected under international law.

The Palestinian Ministry of Foreign Affairs has also condemned the Israeli raid. In a statement, the ministry called the seizure “a flagrant violation of international law and the inviolability, immunities, and privileges of UN facilities”, adding that it constitutes “a dangerous escalation”.

Similarly, the Palestinian National Liberation Movement, or Fatah, condemned the forced displacement of UNRWA’s facilities.

“Targeting UNRWA is a direct attack on the Palestinian refugee issue and a blatant attempt to undermine one of the most important international organisations,” said a statement by the party, which is led by Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas.

Reporting from Ramallah in the occupied West Bank, journalist Sarah Abu Alrob highlighted the severe human impact of the decision. She noted that the centre provided vital services to 16,000 Palestinian refugees who are either in the Qalandiya refugee camp or who visit from across the West Bank.

She said the raid follows a similar operation months ago when Israeli forces raided the UNRWA headquarters in the Sheikh Jarrah neighbourhood of occupied East Jerusalem, where they evacuated the premises and demolished part of the building.

“This comes within a larger campaign where the Israeli government has been calling to dismantle the UNRWA organisation that provides educational, medical and social services to Palestinian refugees who are still in the occupied West Bank,” Abu Alrob said.

Human rights advocates and legal experts have condemned the action. Mohammad Dahleh, a lawyer and human rights advocate from East Jerusalem, described the takeover as a direct breach of international law.

“It’s a clear violation of international law, and it’s a clear violation of the advisory opinion rendered by the International Court of Justice, the highest court in the world, just in December 2025,” Dahleh told Al Jazeera.

“Israel doesn’t care about international law, doesn’t care about the ruling or the advisory opinion of the [UN] International Court of Justice or about the criticism that many countries have against these actions, especially in a period where Palestinian refugees are so vulnerable.”

Dahleh emphasised the critical role that UNRWA has played on the ground during this crisis.

“Palestinian refugees are in a period where they need the assistance that UNRWA is providing the most, whether it’s in occupied Gaza or the occupied West Bank.”

articles.title: Polygamous sect leader gets 24 years in prison for child abuse after girls found in trailer
articles.summary: Samuel Bateman, 50, was convicted of three child abuse counts stemming from an August 2022 traffic stop in Flagstaff that led to the discovery of three girls, ages 11 to 14, in the trailer.
articles.body: PHOENIX — A polygamous sect leader already serving a 50-year federal sentence for orchestrating sex involving children was given another 24 years in prison Tuesday on separate state convictions for child abuse for hauling girls in an unventilated trailer in Arizona. Samuel Bateman, 50, was convicted of three child abuse counts stemming from an August 2022 traffic stop in Flagstaff that led to the discovery of three girls, ages 11 to 14, in the trailer. It had a makeshift toilet, sofa and camping chairs and lacked air conditioning and seat belts. Someone tipped off authorities about the trailer after seeing small fingers reaching through gaps in the doors. Bateman’s small group was an offshoot of the polygamous sect once led by Warren Jeffs. Bateman is currently serving 50 years in federal prison for coercing girls as young as 9 to submit to sex acts with him and other adults and for scheming to kidnap girls from protective custody — the story of which is the focus of the Netflix series, “Trust Me: The False Prophet.” Citing an “insane danger” to the girls in the trailer, among other factors, Judge Joshua Steinlage ordered Bateman to serve the state sentence after completing the 50-year federal sentence. “I love these dear people with all my heart, and I had no intention in the entire world to harm them,” said Bateman, who represented himself in the case and didn’t make a plea for leniency during his sentencing hearing. Victims urged the judge to reject Bateman’s claims that he didn’t mean to harm anyone. One victim who was in the trailer when Bateman was pulled over described the psychological pain she suffered. The victim, who was then 14, said Bateman took advantage of her sexually when she was 12. She said she has had to undergo therapy to recover from “things that should have never happened to me as a child.” “He stole my childhood,” she said. The Associated Press does not typically name alleged victims of sexual assault. Bateman, a self-proclaimed prophet, previously claimed to have more than 20 “spiritual wives,” including 10 girls under the age of 18. In the state case, Bateman acknowledged he knew the girls were in a hot trailer for hours and that the ventilation wasn’t good, but he downplayed the conditions. Bateman had claimed he thought the girls had gotten out when they stopped. He said he was as “shocked as could possibly be” when he learned that they were still inside when he was pulled over. “Today’s sentence is about accountability for the harm done to these young victims,” Coconino County Attorney Ammon Barker said in a statement. “It also ensures that Mr. Bateman will never again be in a position to harm a child.” Federal authorities said Bateman traveled extensively between Arizona, Utah, Colorado and Nebraska as he built an offshoot network of the Fundamentalist Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, which historically has been based in the neighboring communities of Colorado City, Arizona, and Hildale, Utah. He and his followers practiced polygamy, a legacy of the early teachings of the mainstream Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, which abandoned the practice in 1890 and now strictly prohibits it. Bateman was one of the trusted followers of Jeffs, who previously led the sect and is serving a life sentence in Texas for sexual assault of children. The influence of the polygamous sect has waned significantly over time in the towns where the sect has historically been based. In 2017, a court order placed the towns under supervision, excising the church from their governments and shared police department. The area has since transformed so quickly that the towns were released from court-ordered supervision last summer, almost two years earlier than expected. Practicing sect members are now believed to account for only a small percentage of the towns’ populations.

articles.title: Active-duty sergeant’s wife deported to Honduras following Trump’s rollback of protections
articles.summary: Cristy Maryori Villafranca-Trejo is being deported for missing an immigration hearing that according to her husband, Army Sgt. Hedar Leonel Turcios Juarez she was never informed about.
articles.body: The wife of an active-duty U.S. soldier was deported Monday to her native Honduras, according to her family and the U.S. Department of Homeland Security. Cristy Maryori Villafranca-Trejo is at least the seventh spouse or parent of an active-duty U.S. military service member to be deported under President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown. The Associated Press has found more than 50 cases in which immediate family members of U.S. troops were placed in federal immigration detention after the Trump administration rolled back protections for military families. In some instances, DHS has released military spouses following media attention and advocacy by congressional leaders. Villafranca-Trejo’s husband, Army Sgt. Hedar Leonel Turcios Juarez, said he has been struggling to manage his military duties since she was detained July 11 outside a Walmart near Fort Bliss, Texas, where he is stationed. Since then, he’s had to care for their 6-year-old daughter without his wife’s help. Instead of training in the mornings, he takes his daughter to first grade, and he said he has already had to postpone a planned assignment at another base. “I don’t know if I will be able to continue with this,” Turcios Juarez told the AP of his Army career. “I have to make a plan to make sure I can still fulfill my military responsibilities — but also take care of my family.” DHS confirmed Villafranca-Trejo’s deportation, saying she had “received due process.” Villafranca-Trejo, who has no known criminal record and entered the U.S. in 2016 at age 18, was issued a final order of removal by an immigration judge in 2017 after failing to appear at a hearing, according to DHS. Villafranca-Trejo’s husband said she had not received a notice for the hearing she missed and did not realize she had been ordered deported until they went to apply for her green card after marrying in 2022. Originally from Honduras, Turcios Juarez became a U.S. citizen in 2024 after enlisting two years earlier. Villafranca-Trejo’s motion to reopen her case was denied last May and an appeal before the Board of Immigration Appeals remained pending, according to her attorney. She had also been waiting for about a year for a decision on her application for military parole-in-place, a program that allows the immediate family of U.S. troops to remain in the country to apply for a green card. “We were following the rules — we did everything we could on our side to fix this problem,” Turcios Juarez told the AP. Prior to Trump’s second administration, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement would typically allow immediate family members of U.S. troops to adjust their legal status even if they had been issued a final order of removal, according to Dan Gividen, who served as ICE deputy chief counsel from 2016 to 2019 under Trump. “If you’ve got an active-duty military member that’s married to someone now, and that’s going to give her the opportunity to get a green card, you wouldn’t detain them, much less execute the removal order,” Gividen said. JP Caballero, a spokesperson for U.S. Rep. Veronica Escobar, a Democrat representing El Paso, said Escobar had opened a congressional inquiry into Villafranca-Trejo’s case and visited her at the Camp East Montana detention facility in Texas earlier this month. “My heart breaks for her, her children and the soldier who must feel so betrayed by the country he is sacrificing for,” Escobar told the AP in a statement. “There are far too many families like theirs who are being targeted instead of supported.” Turcios Juarez said he is unsure how he will care for his daughter without his wife. He still hasn’t figured out how to tell his daughter what has happened. But he says he still wants to keep serving his country. “I love what I do. I want to keep doing this,” he said of the Army. “I just don’t know how I am going to keep doing this.”

articles.title: Five labourers gunned down at construction site in Pakistan's Balochistan
articles.summary: Pakistan News: Five labourers from Pakistanâs Punjab province were shot dead at a construction site in Balochistanâs Pishin district, a provincial government officia.
articles.body: Five labourers from Pakistanâs Punjab province were shot dead at a construction site in Balochistanâs Pishin district, a provincial government official said Tuesday, according to news agency PTI.The labourers were killed by unidentified gunmen in Saranan town on Monday morning, Balochistan government spokesperson Shahid Rind said. Their bodies were sent to their hometowns in Punjab for burial.Arrangements were made to transport the bodies to their respective villages in Ahmedpur Sharqia and Bahawalpur, Rind said. Security forces have launched a search operation to track down the attackers.Balochistan chief minister Sarfaraz Bugti condemned the killings and vowed action against those responsible."Those shedding the blood of innocent laborers deserve no leniency," Bugti said in a statement issued by his office. "The cowardly acts of terrorists cannot weaken the provincial government's resolve."Saranan town has witnessed militant attacks since last week. A few days ago, gunmen attacked a police station in the town and fled with weapons, ammunition and two vehicles.Banned Baloch insurgent groups have frequently targeted workers and labourers from other provinces working in Balochistan.In July, five barbers from Multan were shot dead in Mashkail town after armed men on motorcycles opened fire at their barber shop.Last month, six labourers from Punjab and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa were abducted in the Nasirabad area of Turbat district. Their bullet-riddled bodies were later found in a remote area, police said.Security and law enforcement agencies have been conducting a large-scale operation against insurgent groups in parts of Balochistan since early July. However, the attacks have continued.In a separate incident on Sunday, five policemen were injured when two unidentified men hurled a hand grenade at a police post in Ambar tehsil of Mohmand district in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.Police retaliated with gunfire, forcing the attackers to flee. The injured policemen were taken to a nearby hospital and are said to be out of danger. articles.title: EasyJet holiday: Dozens stranded in Tunisia after Belfast flight cancelled
articles.summary: One man says he has spent more than £4,000 to get his family of five home after being told they may have to wait 10 days for another flight.
articles.body:
Dozens of people from Northern Ireland have been left stranded in Tunisia after their EasyJet flight home was cancelled, with the airline telling them it had no other flights available for another 10 days.

One man told BBC News NI he has spent £4,000 on travel home for his family-of-five, while another woman, Georgina Doherty, said she and her six children were trying to get home after the death of her mother-in-law.

Others described running out of medication for health issues, while EasyJet were also criticised over a lack of support and communication.

EasyJet has said it is operating an additional direct flight to Belfast on Tuesday night, and that it was "very sorry" for the inconvenience.

BBC News NI understands more than 100 people were booked onto the cancelled flight that was due to leave Enfidha-Hamamet Airport for Belfast International three days ago.

Stuart McCartney, from Dromore, County Down, said he had spent thousands on accommodation and flights to get his family home via a flight to Brussels.

"I'm willing to pay £4,000 to get us home, if needs be, and then battle for reimbursement if I have to after that," he said.

"But we shouldn't have to pay. My holiday was a fraction of what I'm paying to get home right now."

McCartney said EasyJet provided two nights of accommodation but then told the family to find alternative accommodation for the rest of the delay.

He said his mother Katherine, who accompanied his wife and children on the trip, relies on heart medication and they have had to keep a close eye on her remaining supply as the delay continued.

An EasyJet spokesperson said that the company "have been doing everything we can to support Mr McCartney, providing hotel accommodation and meals and we will be reimbursing expenses that may have been incurred".

Georgina Doherty, who is originally from Londonderry but now lives in County Donegal, told BBC News NI the last few days have been an "absolute nightmare" for her family.

Her husband returned home a day before they were due to fly back due to his mother taking ill. She has since died, with Doherty and her six children stranded in Tunisia.

What happened to the EasyJet flight from Tunisia to Belfast?

McCartney said passengers had completed the normal departure process on Saturday night, collecting their boarding passes and gathering at the gate before the flight was called off after more than two hours of delays.

He said the pilot told passengers the aircraft had a number of technical problems, including an issue affecting its steering.

He said "tired and anxious" passengers were eventually taken through the airport in the early hours of Sunday morning and transported by bus to separate hotels.

When he returned to the airport on Sunday, McCartney said an EasyJet agent was only able to look at the airline's own options and could not find a route that would get his family home sooner.

With his children due to return to school and the adults expected back at work, he looked for an alternative. The family are now booked on flights from Tunisia to Brussels, followed by a seven-hour layover before travelling on to Dublin on Wednesday.

He said the uncertainty had taken an emotional toll on his family, particularly his children - he said his son, who is due to return to school and rugby training school, "broke down badly" when he learned of the delay.

Meanwhile, passengers have been supporting each other, he added, helping with transport, translation and finding alternative routes home.

"The camaraderie with people is unbelievable," he added.

"We all are trying so hard for each other."

Like Stuart McCartney, Georgina Doherty and her six children, aged from four to 16, were given two nights accommodation.

On the third day, she said they were told they would have to check out or pay up front for the remainder of our stay.

That would have cost upwards of €3,700 (£3,170), she said.

Doherty said all this was happening as she was trying to tell her children that their "granny had died".

"You couldn't actually have time to process it because we were so stressed out trying to secure the accommodation for the seven of us.

"You couldn't script it, what has happened," she said.

Like many of the passengers, she said, her family has felt abandoned by the airline.

"There has been a complete blackout of communication."

Martine Murray from Belfast, said she is desperate to return home because her mother is seriously ill.

She said she has had to borrow money from friends and family to pay for alternative accommodation after leaving a hotel arranged by EasyJet, which she described as dirty.

"I don't have that money, but I'll have to pay it back," she said.

Murray also has COPD and has run out of her inhaler.

She said she had received an email informing her that her flight had been cancelled, but had been unable to get further information from the airline despite trying to contact it.

"Get us home, we need to get home now," she said.

"I would never travel with them (EasyJet) again."

Natasha Dovbijenko, who is travelling with her husband and child, said the hotel provided by EasyJet was very dirty, with bathrooms that did not work.

Dovbijenko added there was then "a lot of back and forth" over their travel arrangements, including an attempt to separate her from her husband, before they eventually secured a flight to Liverpool.

From there, they had to arrange their own travel back to Ireland.

"There's been no contact from EasyJet, just a message that night saying sorry to hear your flight was cancelled," she said.

"They've treated us very bad. No contact. EasyJet have basically just left us."

EasyJet said the flight to Belfast on 23 August "experienced a technical issue and was unable to operate".

A spokesperson added: "We have been doing everything we can to support our customers, providing hotel accommodation and meals and we will be reimbursing expenses that may have been incurred.

"As alternative flight options including with other carriers are very limited at this busy time of year, we will be operating an additional direct flight from Enfidha to Belfast this evening and providing onward transfers home where needed," the spokeperson said.

The airline said it would be contacting customers directly with the information on the flight.

"A dedicated number - 03305515147 - is also available for customers in Enfidha who require assistance. easyJet holidays customers are also being contacted directly," the spokeperson said.

"The welfare of our customers is our highest priority and we are very sorry for the inconvenience caused."

articles.title: Two killed, refinery on fire in Russia’s Krasnodar after drone attack
articles.summary: Ukraine hits Moscow’s Afipsky oil refinery and Russian-controlled Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant
articles.body:
A fire broke out at the Afipsky oil refinery in Russia’s Krasnodar region following a drone attack, local authorities have said, while two employees at the Russian-controlled Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant were injured in another Ukrainian drone attack.

At least two people were killed, and two others were injured, due to falling drone debris at the Afipsky railway station, Governor Veniamin Kondratyev said on Tuesday.
